events.title: Macedonia divided into four republics
events.summary: At Amphipolis, Aemilius Paullus and ten commissioners proclaimed the Macedonians free, abolished the monarchy and divided the kingdom into four autonomous republics (merides) with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia. Intermarriage and land purchase across their borders were forbidden, the royal gold and silver mines closed, the cutting of ship timber banned, and tribute fixed at half what had been paid to the kings. The royal officials and their sons over fifteen were deported to Italy.
events.detail: Illyria was similarly divided into three districts. Livy (45.18) presents the closure of the mines as protecting the Macedonians from Roman publicani. The mines reopened in 158. The settlement aimed to make Macedon harmless without the cost of direct rule; it lasted until Andriscus.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

events.title: The sack of Epirus
events.summary: On the Senate's orders, Aemilius Paullus punished the Molossians of Epirus, who had sided with Perseus. Roman detachments entered seventy towns simultaneously on a fixed day, collected all valuables, then sacked the towns and enslaved 150,000 people. The proceeds paid the army's donative.
events.detail: Polybius (30.15, preserved by Strabo 7.7.3) and Livy (45.34) record the figures. It was one of the largest enslavements in ancient history and a calculated act of terror; Harris uses it as evidence for Roman brutality and for the economic motive of plunder and slaves.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Ziolkowski, 'Urbs direpta, or how the Romans sacked cities', in Rich & Shipley (eds.), War and Society in the Roman World (1993)
events.debate: The figure of 150,000 may be inflated but is taken seriously by most historians; it fed the slave economy of Italy.

events.title: The thousand Achaean hostages; Polybius in Rome
events.summary: Denounced by the pro-Roman Achaean politician Callicrates, about 1,000 leading Achaeans suspected of sympathy for Perseus were deported to Italy and detained without trial in Etruscan towns for sixteen years. One of them, the former cavalry commander Polybius of Megalopolis, was allowed to stay in Rome, where he became the mentor and friend of the young Scipio Aemilianus and began his Histories.
events.detail: When the 300 survivors were finally released in 150, Cato remarked that the Senate was spending a whole day debating whether some old Greeks should be buried by Italian or Achaean undertakers. The detention embittered Achaean politics and contributed to the war of 146.

events.title: Triumph of Aemilius Paullus
events.summary: Aemilius Paullus' triumph lasted three days: 250 wagons of statues and paintings, then armour, then coin, and finally Perseus walking with his children before the chariot. Five days before, Paullus' 14-year-old son had died, and three days after it his 12-year-old son died too; his two elder sons had been adopted into other families (one became Scipio Aemilianus). Paullus told the people that Fortune had taken her due from his house rather than from the state.
events.detail: Paullus kept nothing for himself except Perseus' library, which he gave to his sons. His soldiers, angry at their share of the booty, nearly blocked the triumph, inspired by Servius Sulpicius Galba. Perseus died in captivity at Alba Fucens a few years later.

events.title: Roman citizens freed from direct tax
events.summary: The Macedonian booty deposited by Paullus was so large that the tributum, the direct property tax paid by Roman citizens to fund war, was no longer levied from 167. Citizens of Italy paid no direct tax again until 43 BC.
events.detail: Pliny (33.56) says Paullus deposited 300 million sesterces; Velleius gives 200 million and Livy's figure (45.40) is lower. The end of tributum shows how empire paid for itself and shifted the fiscal burden to provincials.
events.debate: The booty totals vary by source; the tributum was technically suspended, not abolished.

events.title: Rhodes punished: Delos made a free port
events.summary: Rhodes had tried to mediate between Rome and Perseus, which the Senate took as an affront. Rome stripped Rhodes of Lycia and Caria and gave Delos to Athens as a customs-free port. Rhodian harbour dues fell, according to Rhodian envoys, from a million drachmas a year to 150,000.
events.detail: Polybius (30.31) records the envoys' complaint. Delos became the great slave market of the Aegean, where 10,000 slaves could change hands in a day (Strabo 14.5.2). Rhodes became a formal ally in 164.

events.title: Terence's first comedy
events.summary: Publius Terentius Afer, a former slave from North Africa, staged the Andria at the Megalesian games of 166. His five other comedies followed until 160, the Adelphoe and a second attempt at the Hecyra being performed at the funeral games of Aemilius Paullus.
events.detail: Terence adapted Menander and Apollodorus with a polished style admired by the Scipionic circle; rumours that Scipio Aemilianus or Laelius wrote his plays circulated in his lifetime and he answered them in his prologues.

events.title: Escape of Demetrius from Rome
events.summary: Demetrius, son of Seleucus IV, held as a hostage in Rome since 178, was repeatedly refused permission by the Senate to claim the Seleucid throne after the death of Antiochus IV. With the help of his friend Polybius, who planned the escape, he slipped out of Rome during a hunting party, sailed from Ostia on a Carthaginian ship and seized the throne as Demetrius I Soter.
events.detail: Polybius (31.11-15) tells the story in the first person, one of the most vivid passages of his work.

events.title: Masinissa seizes the Emporia
events.summary: Masinissa occupied the fertile coastal Emporia region of the Lesser Syrtis, claiming it as ancestral land under the 201 treaty. A Roman embassy, Polybius says, ruled in his favour as always, and Carthage lost the towns and paid 500 talents for the revenues.
events.detail: Polybius (31.21) admits that Carthage had the better case but that Roman arbiters favoured Masinissa. Repeated encroachments over the next decade drove Carthage to the war of 150.
events.debate: The date may be 162 or 161; Livy's epitomes place a later dispute in 157.

events.title: Roman treaty with Judas Maccabaeus
events.summary: Judas Maccabaeus, leader of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucids, sent Eupolemus and Jason to Rome and obtained a treaty of friendship and alliance. The Senate wrote warning Demetrius I not to oppress the Jews, Rome's friends.
events.detail: The text of the treaty is given in 1 Maccabees 8 and Josephus. It was a cheap way to weaken the Seleucids and had no immediate practical effect (Judas was killed in 160), but it began a relationship that ended with Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63.
events.debate: Authenticity of the treaty text was once doubted but is now generally accepted, though its wording has been adapted. The Hasmonean polity formally dates from c. 140; the polity tag here anticipates it.

events.title: Senatus consultum expelling philosophers and rhetors
events.summary: A decree of the Senate in the consulship of Gaius Fannius Strabo and Marcus Valerius Messalla authorised the praetor Marcus Pomponius to ensure that no philosophers or rhetoricians remained in Rome.
events.detail: Suetonius and Gellius quote the decree's wording. Like the expulsion of the Epicureans and the reaction to Carneades, it shows a conservative senatorial anxiety about Greek education that never stopped the elite from employing Greek teachers.

events.title: Lex Fannia sumptuaria
events.summary: A sumptuary law of the consul Gaius Fannius Strabo limited the cost of dinners to 100 asses on certain festival days, 30 asses on ten other days a month and 10 asses on ordinary days, restricted the number of guests and forbade serving more than one hen, which must not be fattened.
events.detail: Lucilius mocked the law's 'miserable hundred asses'. Pliny (10.139) notes that the hen clause led Romans to fatten capons instead, a classic example of sumptuary law evasion.

events.title: Death of Aemilius Paullus
events.summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus died after a long illness. His estate was so modest that his widow's dowry could barely be repaid. At his funeral games, organised by his sons Fabius Aemilianus and Scipio Aemilianus, Terence's Adelphoe was staged.

events.title: Censorship of Scipio Nasica Corculum; the first water clock
events.summary: As censor, Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum removed from the Forum all statues of magistrates set up without the authority of the people or Senate, and installed Rome's first public water clock under cover, so that the hour could be told on cloudy days and at night. A Lex Cornelia Fulvia against electoral bribery carried death or exile.

events.title: Dalmatian War: capture of Delminium
events.summary: The Dalmatae, accused of attacking Roman allies Issa and the Daorsi and of insulting Roman envoys, were attacked in 156 by Gaius Marcius Figulus, who failed. In 155 Scipio Nasica Corculum took their stronghold of Delminium by shooting bundles of burning pitch-soaked tow into the town with catapults. Polybius says the Senate wanted to keep Italian soldiers from going soft in peace.

battle.significance: Brought the Dalmatae temporarily to submission; Nasica triumphed.

events.title: Ptolemy VIII bequeaths Cyrene to Rome
events.summary: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, then king of Cyrene and at war with his brother Ptolemy VI, published a will leaving his kingdom to Rome if he died without heirs, to deter assassination and secure Roman support. The will was inscribed in stone at Cyrene.
events.detail: The inscription (SEG IX 7), found in 1929, is the first known royal bequest to Rome and a model for the wills of Attalus III (133), Ptolemy Apion (96) and Nicomedes IV (74). Ptolemy VIII outlived its purpose and it never took effect.

events.title: The embassy of the philosophers
events.summary: Athens, fined 500 talents for sacking Oropus, sent the heads of three philosophical schools to Rome to plead its case: Carneades of the Academy, Diogenes of Babylon of the Stoa and Critolaus of the Peripatos. Their lectures enthralled Roman youth. Carneades spoke one day in praise of justice and the next against it, arguing that if Rome practised justice it would have to return its empire and go back to huts.
events.detail: Cato urged the Senate to decide quickly and send them home before they corrupted the young (Plutarch, Cato 22). The fine was reduced to 100 talents. The episode is a landmark in the reception of Greek philosophy at Rome; Cicero later reworked Carneades' arguments in De re publica 3.

events.title: Lusitanian raids into Ulterior
events.summary: Lusitanians under Punicus raided Roman Ulterior, defeating the praetors Manius Manilius and Lucius Calpurnius Piso with 6,000 Roman dead. Their successor Caesarus defeated Lucius Mummius in 153. The Lusitanian War, with intervals, lasted until 139.

events.title: The first stone theatre demolished
events.summary: The censors Marcus Valerius Messalla and Gaius Cassius Longinus began a permanent stone theatre near the Palatine. On the motion of Scipio Nasica Corculum the Senate ordered it pulled down as harmful to public morals, sold the materials, and for a time forbade seating at plays within a mile of Rome.
events.detail: Rome had no permanent theatre until Pompey's of 55 BC, which was disguised as an approach to a temple of Venus Victrix.

events.title: Consular year begins on 1 January
events.summary: Because of the emergency in Spain, the consuls of 153 took office on 1 January instead of 15 March, so that Quintus Fulvius Nobilior could reach Spain earlier in the campaigning season. The date stuck, and 1 January became the start of the Roman civil year and eventually of ours.

events.title: Cato's embassy to Carthage: 'Carthago delenda est'
events.summary: Cato served on an embassy to arbitrate between Carthage and Masinissa and was alarmed by Carthage's prosperity, manpower and arms. Back in Rome he dropped fresh figs from his toga in the Senate, saying they had been picked three days ago in Carthage, and ended every speech, whatever the subject, by declaring that Carthage must be destroyed. Scipio Nasica Corculum answered each time that Carthage must be preserved, as a check on Roman decadence.
events.detail: The exact formula 'Carthago delenda est' is a later standardisation; Plutarch gives the Greek sense. Whether Rome's motive in 149 was fear, greed, Masinissa's ambitions or Catonian ideology is debated: Harris stresses aggression, Astin traces the debate inside the Senate, and others note that Carthage had nearly finished paying the indemnity in 151.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
events.debate: The date (153 or 152) and Nasica's motives are debated; the figs story is probably authentic in substance.

events.title: Nobilior's defeats: the Vulcanalia and the elephants at Numantia
events.summary: When Segeda of the Belli enlarged its walls in breach of the Gracchan treaties, Quintus Fulvius Nobilior marched with nearly 30,000 men. On 23 August, the feast of the Vulcanalia, the Segedan Carus ambushed his column and killed 6,000 Romans; the day was afterwards held unlucky. Nobilior then attacked the Arevaci at Numantia with ten elephants sent by Masinissa; one was struck by a stone, panicked, and stampeded the others through the Roman ranks, and 4,000 more Romans fell.

sides.strength: c. 30,000 under Q. Fulvius Nobilior with 10 elephants
sides.losses: 6,000 in the ambush and 4,000 at Numantia (Appian)

sides.strength: Belli, Titthi and Arevaci; 20,000 foot, 5,000 horse under Carus

battle.significance: Beginning of twenty years of humiliations for Rome in Celtiberia.

events.title: Foundation of Corduba
events.summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus founded Corduba on the Baetis, the first Roman settlement of its kind in the south and later the capital of Baetica, home of the two Senecas and Lucan. In 152, as consul, Marcellus made a negotiated peace with the Celtiberians that the Senate initially rejected.
events.detail: Polybius (35.2-4) describes the Senate's refusal of Marcellus' peace and the 'fiery war' in Spain; Marcellus nevertheless concluded it on his own terms.
events.debate: Strabo does not date the foundation: it may belong to Marcellus' praetorship (169/168) or to his third consulship (152).

events.title: Levy crisis and the ban on second consulships
events.summary: Terrified by reports of Celtiberian warfare, young Romans evaded the levy for Spain and tribunes imprisoned the consuls Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Aulus Postumius Albinus for refusing exemptions. The 34-year-old Scipio Aemilianus shamed the young nobles by volunteering as military tribune. About this time a law, supported by Cato, forbade anyone to hold the consulship twice.
events.detail: Polybius (35.4) was in Rome and describes the panic. The iteration ban explains why Aemilianus' election in 134 required a special exemption.
events.debate: The date of the law against iteration (c. 152-151) is inferred.

events.title: Lucullus' massacre at Cauca
events.summary: Without provocation or authorisation, Lucius Licinius Lucullus attacked the Vaccaei. Cauca surrendered, paying 100 talents and giving hostages; Lucullus then sent troops inside and massacred the adult males, about 20,000. At Intercatia Scipio Aemilianus killed a Spanish champion in single combat and was first over the wall, winning the mural crown; at Pallantia Lucullus failed.
events.detail: Appian (Iberica 52) says Lucullus was never brought to account. The episode, with Galba's massacre a year later, fuelled the movement for an extortion court.

battle.significance: A byword for Roman bad faith in Spain.

events.title: Galba's massacre of the Lusitanians
events.summary: Servius Sulpicius Galba, praetor in Ulterior, promised the Lusitanians good land if they laid down their arms, divided them into three groups, disarmed them and then had them slaughtered. Suetonius gives 30,000 victims. Among the few survivors was a young herdsman named Viriathus.
events.detail: Prosecuted in 149 by the tribune Lucius Scribonius Libo, with the 85-year-old Cato speaking against him in his last speech, Galba won acquittal by tearfully presenting his young children and an orphaned ward to the people. Cicero thought him the greatest orator of his age. The scandal helped carry the Lex Calpurnia.

battle.significance: Produced Viriathus and a decade of war.

events.title: Carthage's war with Masinissa
events.summary: Provoked beyond endurance, Carthage raised an army under Hasdrubal and fought Masinissa, now 88 and still riding without a saddle, near Oroscopa. Surrounded in a hilltop camp, starved and diseased, the Carthaginians surrendered, but Gulussa's Numidian cavalry massacred them as they left disarmed. Scipio Aemilianus, in Africa to obtain elephants for Lucullus, watched from a hill.
events.detail: By waging war without Roman permission Carthage breached the treaty of 201, giving Rome its pretext. Appian gives 58,000 Carthaginians, few of whom returned.

sides.strength: 25,400 foot and 400 horse plus later levies (Appian)
sides.losses: most of the army killed after surrender

battle.significance: Carthage's breach of the 201 treaty became Rome's casus belli.
